title: "Its not far off of a sort of movie opera": The Return of the King at 20

commenti.body:
I really hate the snobbishness this sub can have towards modern masterpieces. 

If recency bias can used as a reason to dismiss a film, then nostalgia bias should be used as a measurement as well. 

Lord of the Rings brought a depth to the cinematic landscape that had yet to be captured before. The closest film I could compare it to is Lawrence of Arabia, in terms of both masterful world-building and epic scope. It’s ability to intertwine riveting dialogue, with hand-crafted exposition is very underrated.

The trilogy is perhaps still the best cinematic showing of a fantastic universe that is not our own. Credit is due for the design of places like Wakanda or Pandora, but the combination of deeply felt character writing, excellent special (practical) effects and a deep love for the material shine through all throughout these films. They are operatic, certainly, but also epic in the literary sense of the word.
Just curious (as someone who quite enjoys the film, with a few caveats) -- what do you mean by depth here?

> If recency bias can be used as a reason to dismiss a film, then nostalgia bias should be used as a measurement as well.   

At 20 years, Return of the King *is* subject to nostalgia bias.
In the behind the scenes on RotK Peter Jackson said he wanted to do David Lean meets Harryhausen, which is a great deacription.

Yeah, and it’s not as if critics hated it when it came out, either. I recall Roger Ebert liked the movies a lot. They’re sweeping and majestic, and manage to achieve a real sense of dramatic weight despite the ostensible silliness of the fantasy world depicted. Like the best epics, it situates human-scale narrative and emotion in a huge world. Consider Theoden, who’s not even one of the principal characters but whose story is meaningful (even if the whole redemption-through-sacrifice thing is older than dirt, which I suppose isn’t necessarily a mark against it). If Aragorn’s speech before the black gate doesn’t get you, you don’t have a pulse (or at least you’re not a western male with a pulse). Sure, that kind of thing’s an old standby of war films, but again, that the movies are in touch with our cinematic and cultural traditions is no crime.

How is that bit very underrated? Could you expand on that. I'm thinking of Syd Field, screenwriting authority who praises the (expository) opening sequence of fellowship in his book. Iirc gandalf does a bit of exposition and mckellan's performance was widely praised

> I recall Roger Ebert liked the movies a lot.

Well, he didn't give the full four stars to any one of them, and he's usually not very shy of giving a film four stars. He also has quite a few points of criticism of them in his reviews.

> That "Fellowship of the Ring" doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours. Perhaps it will look exactly as you think it should. But some may regret that the Hobbits have been pushed out of the foreground and reduced to supporting characters. And the movie depends on action scenes much more than Tolkien did. 

-----------

> "The Two Towers" will possibly be more popular than the first film, more of an audience-pleaser, but hasn't Jackson lost the original purpose of the story somewhere along the way? He has taken an enchanting and unique work of literature and retold it in the terms of the modern action picture. If Tolkien had wanted to write about a race of supermen, he would have written a Middle-Earth version of "Conan the Barbarian." But no. He told a tale in which modest little hobbits were the heroes. And now Jackson has steered the story into the action mainstream. To do what he has done in this film must have been awesomely difficult, and he deserves applause, but to remain true to Tolkien would have been more difficult, and braver.

-------------

> There is little enough psychological depth anywhere in the films, actually, and they exist mostly as surface, gesture, archetype and spectacle. They do that magnificently well, but one feels at the end that nothing actual and human has been at stake; cartoon characters in a fantasy world have been brought along about as far as it is possible for them to come, and while we applaud the achievement, the trilogy is more a work for adolescents (of all ages) than for those hungering for truthful emotion thoughtfully paid for.

There's a melancholic, downbeat tone to much of the book -- the days of elves and magic and, well, cool shit are over, all that wonder is passing from the world. Even when, yeah, Aragorn restores the kingdom,  it's a shadow of past glories that will eventually become as  mundane as anything else in the world of men (sic). The ring-bearers leave for the Isle of Avalon, as it were, and the heroes that stay behind never in  the rest of their lives face anything remotely as important or real as what they've done in the book. Never again will they be so *alive*.

It's one way LotR is different from so many of Tolkien's epigones, that the cool exciting adventure-y stuff is always leavened with this sadness at how it will never come again, it's almost a mono no aware for the very idea of adventure. Middle Earth is that rare vast fantasy setting that *doesn't* promise a million more adventures just around the corner, where the sky's the limit. Rather, by the end of LotR, the skies are *already* limited, and adventures all but over. There's a reason that Amazon thing is a prequel, not a sequel
